title: Oliver's sidemen, sustained notes, Chicago change, and diabetes
summary: Souchon names sidemen and says no record shows Oliver's single sustained note. In Chicago Oliver had changed his style and added saxes. Ory's West Coast group came closest to the old sound. Souchon suspects Oliver had diabetes.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Exactly the same way. The personnel of the band was something that was interesting, too. I remember Ori playing with them. I remember Johnny Dodds. I don't remember Baby Dodds playing with them. If he did, I don't remember it. Bob Foster played with them sometimes. And then what's this other bass down here? It was either of those two were always in demand. Ed Garland. Ed Garland. Garland, but there was still another one. I don't remember. There's so many of them around here. I remember something that none of the records ever... Nothing that Oliver ever did on any of the records approached his real peak at the time. He could take one note and sustain that through a whole damn chorus of the band doing the changes behind it. Just one. He'd just hold it just as clean and pure as you ever heard.
I never heard that on a record. No.

And as I say, hearing him again in Chicago, he had completely changed his style. He was trying to play like a white band. They were even adding instruments, a couple of saxes and all. They had lost it. And people went nuts about it. It's the closest thing to an example of it that they had. But I would say the Ory group out on the West Coast when they had... Who was the little trumpet player?
Mud Carey. And was it Joe Darnsberg? Yeah, Joe Darnsberg. Joe Darnsberg. And Bud Scott.

That is the closest thing to the old type of music that Bud... That Oliver played in those days. Yes, yes. They were dressed up and they were big shots and all that. And the attitude was very nice. I mean, the one that was pretty much of a... felt his oats very much was Baby Todd's when he was in Chicago. But Oliver was just as cordial and nice as he could be. Incidentally, from a doctor's standpoint, I am convinced that he had diabetes. Yeah, you told me that, Mark. Because the fact that he would drink these buckets of sugar water he had next to the band. He'd just sop that up. It's a craving for sweets.
And he was a terrible eater, as the story goes.
Oh, yeah. He really must have been. He wouldn't talk that way.
